A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
transfer
Money moved between bank accounts.
accountant
A person who checks financial records.
authorisation
Official permission to carry out an action.
courier
A service that delivers documents or parcels.
confidential
Kept private and not shared publicly.
correction
A published statement fixing an earlier mistake.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The next morning, Fiona Bell called Emma with news about the matching reference. An independent accountant had examined the banking record behind it. The first transfer had been returned by the bank. A later transfer had gone into an account controlled by the Glenarraidh Education Trust, not directly to a student. The trust's exception book marked the case as resolved.

“Does that mean the student never got the money?” Emma asked.

“We cannot say that,” Fiona replied. “The records we have do not show what happened after the money reached the trust's account.”

There was a second finding. A signed approval sheet linked to the same reference carried Malcolm Vale's full name. The accountant had checked it against signed trust documents from 2011.

“So Malcolm approved that transfer?”

“The evidence supports that one approval. It does not tell us what he intended, or what happened to every other grant.”

Emma told Sarah. At last they could report a real difference between an approval, a bank transfer and a payment received by a student. They still could not call it theft.

Then Fiona sent another document, this time from 2026. It was an email from Malcolm's work account, with the exact words of the second letter Emma had received. The message instructed a colleague to send it in Claire's name. Courier records matched the delivery. Emma and Sarah checked the dates and the wording independently.

“The warning letter wasn't from Claire,” Sarah said.

“Now we have evidence of who arranged it,” Emma replied.

They contacted Malcolm and gave him an opportunity to answer. He admitted arranging the second letter. He said he had wanted Emma to stop upsetting people connected with the trust. He denied taking student money and said the finances would be explained. Emma recorded both his admission and his denial.

That evening Fiona asked whether Emma would accept a private call. Claire Morrison wanted to speak.

Emma sat very still as the screen lit up. The woman looked older than in the 2011 photograph, but Emma knew her voice. Claire showed her the original draft and courier details of the first letter, written on 14 October 2026. They also checked private details with James Morrison, without asking him to reveal Claire's location.

“I sent the first letter,” Claire said. “Not the second.”

“Why did you leave?” Emma asked.

“I was frightened. I thought the trust was calling some grants paid before the students had received them. I asked questions, and I felt that my brother and the students might suffer if I stayed. Daniel Reid helped me leave on 21 September 2011. He didn't take me against my will, and he doesn't know where I live now.”

Emma remembered Nora seeing Claire enter a car. Claire had chosen to get in, but that did not mean she had felt safe staying in the village.

“I wrote that you left after a personal argument,” Emma said quietly. “I was wrong. I didn't check enough.”

“You can correct it now,” Claire answered. “But please don't tell people where I am. And let me speak to James myself.”

Emma promised to respect that choice.

The following day the newspaper published a carefully checked report. It explained the one documented transfer into the trust's account, Malcolm's signed authorisation and the forged warning letter. It also published a correction to Emma's old story. The newspaper asked for an independent review of the remaining grants. It did not claim that every student had lost money or reveal Claire's address.

James read the correction. He did not forgive Emma immediately, but he thanked her for finally changing the headline.

In the investigation file, Emma left the early anonymous calls and message marked ‘sender unknown’. Reid's admission still needed an official response. The students' remaining payment questions belonged in the wider review, not in a guessed ending.

That night Emma put Claire's first letter beside the new article. The mystery had not ended with every bank account explained. It had ended with a false story corrected, a real woman heard, and questions that could finally be investigated openly.

Emma folded the letter carefully. She no longer needed to guess what it meant.
